title: Worksheet — School Kitchen Garden (Class 6 CBSE Vocational Education)
instructions: Attempt all 11 questions. Show your reasoning where required. Total time: 50 minutes.

questions.question: A kitchen garden is a small garden where you grow:
How many main growing seasons are there in India?
Watering at noon is best for kitchen-garden plants.
questions.explanation: Early morning or late afternoon is best.

questions.question: A small hand-hoe used for digging and weeding is called a ____.
Which is a SAFE pest-management method for a school garden?
options: picking caterpillars by hand or using mild neem-water
questions.answer: picking caterpillars by hand or using mild neem-water

questions.question: If you plan to grow spinach, coriander and peas at school, which season fits best?
What is a kitchen garden? List THREE benefits of having one at school.
questions.answer: A kitchen garden is a small garden where you grow plants you can eat. Three benefits: (i) fresh, safe, nutritious food; (ii) you learn planning, observation, patience and care; (iii) attracts bees and butterflies for pollination and makes the school greener. (Also: shared harvests build friendship.)

questions.question: Name the three main Indian growing seasons and give one example crop for each.
questions.answer: (i) Kharif (June/July sowing) — gourds, brinjal, beans. (ii) Rabi (Oct/Nov sowing) — spinach, coriander, peas. (iii) Zaid (Mar/Apr sowing) — cucumber, watermelon.

questions.question: Explain the three main ways to start a plant in a kitchen garden.
questions.answer: (i) Direct sowing — drop the seed straight into the bed (e.g. spinach, coriander, radish). (ii) Seedlings — start seeds in a small tray, then transplant the small plants into the bed (e.g. tomato, brinjal, chilli). (iii) Cuttings — put a stem cutting into moist soil so it grows roots (e.g. mint, curry leaves).

questions.question: Your school has a small empty plot of about 5×5 m. Plan a Rabi kitchen garden for it. Describe: (i) which crops you will grow and why, (ii) where you will place each, (iii) what tools you will use, (iv) one risk you must plan for.
questions.answer: (i) For a 5×5 m Rabi plot I will grow spinach, coriander, peas, radish and pots of mint — easy short-cycle crops suited to the cool months and giving a mix of leaves, pulse and root for the school kitchen. (ii) Tall pea plants on the north so they don't shade smaller plants; spinach and coriander in long rows in the middle; radish in a short row in front (south); mint in pots so it doesn't spread. Leave a one-foot path between rows. (iii) Tools — khurpi, trowel, watering can, small rake, gloves, wooden tags. Soil mixed with compost (2:1). (iv) Risk: caterpillars eating leaves. Plan: inspect leaves twice a week, pick caterpillars by hand, plant marigolds at the corners, keep mild neem-water spray ready.

questions.question: After two weeks of caring for your kitchen garden you find small holes in some leaves and the soil is dry every morning. What might be wrong and what would you do? Use ideas from the chapter.
questions.answer: Two problems likely: (1) holes in leaves suggest pests — caterpillars or aphids. (2) dry soil every morning suggests too little watering or watering at the wrong time. Plan: (a) Inspect leaves carefully, turn them over, look for caterpillars, eggs or aphids; pick caterpillars by hand; spray a mild neem-water solution; plant marigolds nearby for the future. (b) Water early morning so the soil stays moist through the day; check soil before watering — if already moist, skip; mulch with dry leaves to lock in moisture. (c) Record both problems and the steps in the garden diary so I can see if they help over the next week. Reflection turns problems into learning.
